paragraphs.heading: What the geodynamo is
paragraphs.text: The geodynamo is the process that makes Earth's magnetic field. Dynamo theory explains how a body like Earth or a star produces such a field: a fluid that rotates, convects and conducts electricity can keep a field going over astronomical timescales. In Earth that fluid is the liquid iron of the outer core, whose convection induces the field and constantly keeps it up. A dynamo is also thought to be behind the fields of Mercury and the Jovian planets.

paragraphs.heading: A long search for the cause
paragraphs.text: In 1600 William Gilbert concluded in De Magnete that Earth is magnetic, and suggested it was permanently magnetised, like lodestone. In 1822 André-Marie Ampère proposed currents inside Earth instead, and in 1919 Joseph Larmor proposed a dynamo. Applying Carl Friedrich Gauss's theories to magnetic measurements showed that the field comes from inside Earth rather than outside. Elsasser, seen as a father of today's dynamo theory, proposed that the field comes from electric currents induced in the fluid outer core.

paragraphs.heading: What keeps it running
paragraphs.text: Left alone, the field would fade through ohmic decay, which for the dipole field would take about 20,000 years. So the outer core must keep convecting, probably through a mix of heat-driven and composition-driven flow. Its heat comes from the core being compressed by gravity, from light elements being pushed out at the edge of the growing inner core, from heat given off as that edge crystallises, and from radioactive potassium, uranium and thorium. The mantle controls how fast heat leaves the core.

paragraphs.heading: Spin organises the flow
paragraphs.text: The fluid also has to rotate. Earth's spin supplies this through the Coriolis effect, which tends to line up fluid motions and electric currents in columns parallel to the rotation axis. Its rise or decay follows what is called the induction equation: ∂𝐁/∂t = η∇²𝐁 + ∇ × (𝐮 × 𝐁). Comparing its two right-hand terms gives the magnetic Reynolds number, which weighs how strongly the flow carries the field along against how fast the field diffuses away.

paragraphs.heading: Modelling it on computers
paragraphs.text: At the start of the 21st century, computer models of Earth's field were still far from precise. Early models could produce a strong, Earth-like field only by assuming the same temperature everywhere on the core's surface and an extremely viscous core fluid. Models with more realistic values gave less Earth-like fields, yet suggested that refining them might one day work. Tiny temperature differences of a few millikelvins across the core's surface greatly boost the flow and give more realistic fields.

paragraphs.heading: Dynamos on other worlds
paragraphs.text: A dynamo needs a liquid interior that conducts electricity. Tidal heating, where tidal forces between orbiting bodies cause friction that warms their insides, can help keep an interior liquid. Jupiter's moon Io and Saturn's moon Enceladus have enough of it to melt their inner cores, but they may not have dynamos because they cannot conduct electricity. Mercury, though small, has a magnetic field, because its iron make-up and the friction from its very elliptical orbit give it a conductive liquid core.
